By stating 5.44% plainly, the real advantages — much lower activation, lighter shielding, direct conversion, low water — stand on solid ground. Candor about the neutron fraction is what makes the rest of the resource case defensible.

The commercial temptation to say 'aneutronic' is exactly why the discipline matters. A single overstated word would put every adjacent claim — lower activation, lighter shielding, direct conversion, low water — under suspicion. Stating 5.44% plainly costs nothing real and buys credibility for the genuine, substantial advantages the low neutron fraction delivers relative to a D-T machine.

title: Deuterium from Water
lede: Deuterium, a fuel for both machines, is separated from ordinary water and is effectively unlimited at any plausible deployment scale.
body: Deuterium is a heavy isotope of hydrogen and a primary fuel for both the D-T breeder (Hyperion) and the D-<sup>3</sup>He burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). It occurs naturally in ordinary water — a small, fixed fraction of all hydrogen — and is separated by established industrial processes. For the resource question, deuterium is effectively unlimited.

Every liter of water contains deuterium. The fraction is small per liter, but the total in the world's water is enormous relative to any conceivable fusion deployment. There is no mining, no depletion concern, and no geopolitically concentrated deposit. This is one of the strongest, most defensible resource claims in fusion.
Deuterium: abundant in water, no supply constraint.
The water used to source deuterium is negligible against the water discussion elsewhere on this site.
Tritium for the breeder is bred in the lithium blanket, not mined.
Helium-3 for the burner is the genuine supply constraint, treated on its own page.

The defensible statement is unambiguous: deuterium is an effectively unlimited fuel drawn from water, with no meaningful resource or water penalty for its extraction. This is the easy end of the fusion fuel-resource spectrum; the hard end is helium-3.

It is worth closing the loop with the water discussion elsewhere on this site: the water consumed to extract deuterium is negligible against a plant's operational cooling water, and vanishingly small against the world's water resource. So deuterium is not only an unlimited fuel, it carries no meaningful water penalty in its sourcing — a rare case where a resource is both abundant and cheap to obtain in environmental terms.

title: The Helium-3 Supply Gate
lede: The burner's helium-3 demand is roughly 400x domestic supply per commercial unit, a hard resource gate that shapes the whole deployment path.
body: The single largest resource constraint in the Kronos program is stated plainly here. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) burns helium-3, and a commercial unit would demand roughly 400 times current domestic helium-3 supply. Helium-3 does not exist at terrestrial scale in the quantities a fleet of burners would need. This is a physics-and-supply fact, not an economics statement, and it is a hard gate.

Helium-3 is extraordinarily rare on Earth. Present terrestrial supply comes mostly as a by-product of tritium decay in limited stockpiles — small, and already spoken for by other uses. There is no natural terrestrial deposit at energy scale. A single commercial burner's appetite dwarfs this supply by about 400x.
Why breeder-bred and lunar helium-3 matter
The breeder (Hyperion) co-produces helium-3 at roughly the ~1.97 kg/yr class, a partial terrestrial pathway.
Lunar regolith holds helium-3 implanted by the solar wind, the only known large reservoir.
Without one or both, commercial burner deployment is fuel-gated, full stop.
This is a supply-existence gate, a physics fact rather than an economic one; we make no economic statement about it.

Stating this gate openly is essential to honesty. The burner's water and land advantages are real, but the machine is gated on a fuel that does not yet exist at terrestrial scale. The breeder's helium-3 co-production and lunar sourcing are the strategic answers, and both are long-horizon. This is the most important resource caveat on the site.

title: The Breeder-Bred Helium-3 Pathway
lede: The breeder co-produces helium-3, providing a terrestrial pathway toward the burner's fuel, though far below fleet-scale demand.
body: One answer to the helium-3 supply gate is to make it. The breeder (Hyperion) co-produces helium-3 at roughly the ~1.97 kg/yr class, alongside its ~4 kg/yr-class tritium and 14 MeV neutrons. This is a genuine terrestrial pathway to the fuel the burner needs — but it must be understood in proportion to the ~400x gate.

The breeder's D-T operation breeds tritium in its lithium blanket. Tritium decays to helium-3 over time; captured and separated, that helium-3 becomes burner fuel. So the two machines form a chain: the breeder makes the fuel the burner consumes, on Earth, without mining.
Breeder co-production (~1.97 kg/yr class) is a partial pathway, not a full solution to the ~400x gate.
Scaling to a burner fleet from breeder co-production alone would require a very large breeder fleet.
This is why lunar helium-3 remains part of the long-horizon strategy alongside breeder co-production.
All figures are design-and-simulation values for unbuilt machines.

The defensible framing is that the breeder provides a real, terrestrial, non-mined helium-3 pathway that partially closes the supply gate, while acknowledging honestly that it does not by itself reach fleet-scale burner demand. The full answer combines breeder co-production with lunar helium-3 over a long horizon.

The proportion is the honest crux. Breeder co-production at the ~1.97 kg/yr class is a real, terrestrial, non-mined source of helium-3, but a single commercial burner's demand is roughly 400x current domestic supply, so co-production from a modest breeder fleet closes only part of the gap. This is precisely why the strategy pairs breeder co-production with long-horizon lunar helium-3 rather than relying on either alone.

title: Lunar Helium-3 Context
lede: Lunar regolith is the only known large helium-3 reservoir; it is a long-horizon resource, described honestly without overclaiming.
body: The only known reservoir of helium-3 large enough to matter for energy is not on Earth. The solar wind has implanted helium-3 into the Moon's regolith over billions of years. This is the resource that could, in principle, close the burner's fuel gate at fleet scale — and it is deliberately described here as a long-horizon prospect, not a near-term supply.
What is real and what is not yet
Real: helium-3 is present in lunar regolith, implanted by the solar wind, and is the largest known reservoir.
Not yet: extraction, processing, and return of lunar helium-3 at energy scale is unproven and far off.
Honest: this is a strategic reason the burner's fuel path points to the Moon, not a claim that lunar fuel is available.
Complementary: near-term terrestrial helium-3 comes from breeder co-production, not the Moon.

We describe lunar helium-3 as context, not capability. The concentration in regolith is low, requiring large volumes of processed material per unit of helium-3, and the logistics of lunar surface operations and return are formidable. None of this is solved; all of it is long-horizon.
Why it belongs on a resources page

A complete, honest resource account for the burner cannot end at the ~400x terrestrial gate; it must name the reservoir that could resolve it. Lunar helium-3 is that reservoir. We state its scale and its long-horizon, unproven status together, so the strategic logic is clear without overclaiming availability.

title: Tritium Breeding as a Design Lever
lede: The breeder makes its own tritium in a lithium blanket; the breeding ratio is a design lever, and self-sufficiency at the low end is an open question.
body: Tritium is radioactive and scarce in nature, so a D-T machine that had to buy tritium would face a supply wall. The breeder (Hyperion) avoids this by breeding its own tritium in a lithium blanket. How much it breeds relative to how much it burns is the tritium breeding ratio, treated across design values of 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.

A breeding ratio above 1.0 means the plant makes more tritium than it consumes, allowing self-sufficiency plus a surplus (the ~4 kg/yr-class product) to start other machines or supply other uses. The ratio is a lever because it depends on blanket design, neutron multiplication, and coverage — engineering choices, not a fixed constant.
At TBR 1.1, self-sufficiency is tight and depends on minimizing losses; this is an open reconciliation, not a settled result.
Higher ratios need effective neutron multiplication (e.g., beryllium), raising the multiplier-material question.
Local blanket breeding versus net plant self-sufficiency is a distinction we do not blur.
All values are design-and-simulation; blanket breeding is not yet demonstrated at plant scale.

The defensible framing is that tritium supply for the breeder is solved in principle by breeding — the fuel is made, not mined — while the margin at the low end of the breeding-ratio lever is a genuine open design question. We present the lever honestly rather than asserting a settled self-sufficiency.

title: Siting Criteria Overview
lede: Water, land, grid, security, and permitting jointly determine where a plant can be built; water-light, compact designs widen the options.
body: Siting a power plant is a multi-constraint problem. Water availability, land footprint, grid access, security, workforce, and permitting all have to be satisfied at once. A design that relaxes one of the hardest constraints — water — without worsening the others widens the set of feasible sites. This page frames how the Kronos machines sit within those constraints.
Water: availability for cooling and makeup; the burner relaxes this via direct conversion.
Land: footprint plus setbacks and interconnection; compact plants relax this.
Grid: interconnection for backup and export; co-location reduces corridor land.
Security: relevant especially for Aegis on defense installations.
Permitting: environmental review covering water, land, air, and radiological aspects.

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) does well on water and land and can co-locate with load, but is bounded by the availability gate (~0.86-0.995) for the most uptime-critical sites. The breeder (Hyperion) is compact but carries a thermal load, so water availability or a dry-cooling choice enters its siting.

We present siting as a balance, not a marketing point. The machines relax the water and land constraints meaningfully, which is a real siting advantage, while the availability gate and the helium-3 fuel gate remain honest bounds on where and when the burner can be deployed. The land and water pages give the mechanisms behind each constraint.

The value of framing siting as a balance is that it prevents any single advantage from being oversold. The machines relax the water and land constraints in ways that genuinely widen the feasible-site map, while the availability gate and the helium-3 fuel gate remain honest bounds on which loads the burner can serve and when a fleet can be deployed. A credible site selection satisfies all of these at once.

title: Environmental Permitting: Water and Land Scope
lede: Fusion plants are subject to standard environmental permitting for water, land, and discharge; compactness and low water reduce the scope, not the obligation.
body: A fusion plant is not exempt from environmental review. Like any facility touching a watershed or occupying land, it is subject to permitting covering water withdrawal and discharge, land disturbance, air, noise, and radiological aspects. The honest position is that the machines' water and land characteristics reduce the scope of some reviews while the obligation to be reviewed remains fully in place.
Water withdrawal permits: minimal for the water-light burner; cooling-choice dependent for the breeder.
Discharge permits: no bulk thermal discharge from the burner; managed for a wet-cooled breeder.
Land disturbance and stormwater: standard construction-phase permitting, bounded by the compact footprint.
Radiological aspects: governed separately under the appropriate byproduct-material framework.

Because the burner has no large withdrawal and no bulk discharge, its water-permitting scope is genuinely lighter. Because both plants are compact, land-disturbance permitting covers a smaller area. These are reductions in scope, honestly framed, not exemptions.

We do not claim streamlined or waived permitting; that is a regulatory outcome we do not pre-empt. The defensible statement is that the physical characteristics — no large withdrawal, no bulk discharge, compact footprint — reduce the scope of the water and land reviews, while every applicable review still applies to the design-and-simulation machines as they mature toward licensing.

The radiological aspect is where scope is not reduced. Both machines are neutron sources and handle activated materials and, for the breeder, a bounded tritium inventory, so the applicable radiological review applies in full and is governed under the appropriate byproduct-material framework. Presenting the water and land scope as reduced while the radiological scope is unchanged is the honest, complete picture.

title: Resource Supply-Chain Resilience
lede: Fusion's fuel is abundant or bred, but its specialty materials have concentrated supply chains that are the real resilience question.
body: Resource resilience has two halves: fuel and materials. Fusion is strong on fuel — deuterium from water, tritium bred on-site, lithium abundant — with helium-3 the notable exception. The materials half is where concentrated supply chains, not raw scarcity, pose the resilience question.
Deuterium: effectively unlimited, from water, no supply risk.
Tritium: bred in the breeder's blanket, not mined; supply is a design question, not a geopolitical one.
Lithium: abundant, though it competes with battery demand.
Helium-3: the exception — ~400x gated, addressed by breeder co-production and lunar sourcing.

The specialty materials — REBCO superconductor, beryllium, tungsten — have geographically concentrated supply chains. The resilience issue is manufacturing capacity and geographic concentration, not that the elements are running out. Diversifying superconductor manufacturing and multiplier-material choices are the levers.

The defensible statement is that fusion's fuel resilience is a real strength — abundant or bred — with helium-3 the acknowledged exception, and that the materials resilience challenge is supply-chain concentration and manufacturing scale-up rather than fundamental scarcity. Both halves are stated plainly so the resource picture is complete.

The two halves of resilience call for different responses. Fuel resilience is largely a design achievement — abundant deuterium, bred tritium, abundant lithium — with helium-3 the acknowledged exception addressed by breeding and lunar sourcing. Materials resilience is an industrial and geographic problem, addressed by scaling superconductor manufacturing and diversifying multiplier-material choices, not by finding more of a scarce element.

title: Water, Land, and Resource Profile: Summary
lede: A consolidated, honest view: the burner is water-light and land-light by architecture, the breeder is compact but cooling-dependent, and both carry stated gates.
body: This page consolidates the water, land, and resource story for both machines in one honest view. The pattern throughout is architectural advantages that are real, paired with gates that are stated plainly rather than softened.

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is water-light because direct energy conversion removes the steam-cycle condenser — the dominant water demand of a thermal plant — leaving only modest, closed-loop residual heat. The breeder (Hyperion) carries a real thermal load and its water use depends on cooling choice (wet versus dry). Neither claim is a published water number; both are architecture-level and design-and-simulation based.

Both machines are compact, high-power-density plants whose footprint is buildings and setbacks, not a collection field. Co-location with load (Aegis on defense installations, MetroVolt at data centers) avoids transmission-corridor land. Brownfield reuse is feasible. The land case is comparative and mechanism-based, not a numeric superiority claim.
Fuel: deuterium unlimited, tritium bred, lithium abundant; helium-3 is ~400x gated.
Materials: mostly common and recyclable; specialty supply chains (REBCO, beryllium, tungsten) are the resilience issue.
Gates stated plainly: helium-3 supply, burner availability (~0.86-0.995 vs Tier III 0.99982), plug-coil and plug-regime physics gates.
Timeline: breeder construction begins Q2 2027, FOAK first tritium ~2030; no hardware net-gain claim before FOAK.

The honest bottom line: the water and land advantages are genuine and architectural, the fuel and materials picture is strong except for the helium-3 gate, and the availability and physics gates are real bounds. Stating advantages and gates together is what makes the whole profile defensible.

title: Honest Gates and the Resource Case
lede: The four canonical burner gates are physics facts, not economics; stating them alongside the water and land advantages is what earns trust.
body: The water, land, and resource advantages on this site are real, but they sit beside four honest gates for the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). These are physics-and-engineering findings from design-and-simulation studies, never economic statements. Presenting them plainly, next to the advantages, is the whole point of full-candor communication.
Plug coil overstressed ~3-3.9x at the design bore — infeasible as specified; a magnet-engineering gate.
Plug operating regime 166-830x beyond any existing device — un-post-dictable today; a plasma-physics gate.
Helium-3 fuel demand ~400x domestic supply per commercial unit — gated on a fuel that does not exist at terrestrial scale.
Availability ~0.86-0.995 versus hyperscale Tier III 0.99982 — 30-100x short on downtime; not a sole Tier-III source today.

None of these is ever expressed as an economic or monetary figure of any kind; they are stated as the physical and supply facts they are. Two of them — the helium-3 gate and the availability gate — bear directly on the resource and siting story and are treated in depth on their own pages.

The breeder (Hyperion) advances first — construction from Q2 2027, FOAK first tritium ~2030 — and there is no hardware net-gain claim before FOAK. The burner's real water and land advantages do not erase its gates, and pretending otherwise would forfeit credibility. Stating both in the same breath is what makes the environment, health, and safety case trustworthy.

title: Defensible Claims and Rejected Comparisons
lede: This repo publishes only solid, public, mechanism-based environmental claims; a scale-mismatched 'cleaner than X' comparison was rejected.
body: Not every plausible-sounding environmental claim is defensible, and this page documents the discipline applied here. The rule is simple: publish only claims that rest on a specific mechanism, a public baseline, and a fair comparison. Claims that rely on a scale mismatch or an unbuilt-plant number are rejected.
Architecture claims: direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle, so the burner is water-light. Mechanism-based.
Class claims: fusion plants are compact, high-power-density generators. Physically grounded.
Mechanism-avoidance: no large withdrawal means no intake mortality; no bulk discharge means no thermal plume.
Fuel-resource claims: deuterium is unlimited; helium-3 is ~400x gated. Both stated together.

An internal comparison asserting that one machine is categorically cleaner than a named alternative was rejected because it relied on a scale mismatch — comparing quantities defined on different bases. We do not publish it. We also do not publish water- or land-intensity numbers for unbuilt machines, because a single figure would imply a measured result that does not exist for a design-and-simulation study.

Credibility is the asset this repo protects. Every honest gate stated elsewhere — helium-3, availability, plug physics — is only believable because the positive claims are equally disciplined. By publishing mechanism-based, same-basis, design-and-simulation-framed claims and rejecting scale-mismatched ones, the water, land, and resource case stays defensible under scrutiny.
